passage:
At the tenants’ meeting in Porto, the hall clapped for Rafael, who spoke about rising rents in a loud, sure voice. I’m Paulo, and I had come only to hand out flyers, and I felt small.
Then I noticed Marta by the door, printing leaflets and refilling the paper without a word. Ines was writing letters to the council at a side table. Old Joaquim slipped money into the jar for the hall’s hire. Nobody clapped for any of them.
I had been resenting Rafael’s spotlight. Then Rafael turned and said, “Without Marta’s leaflets, nobody would be here.” Marta shrugged, pleased. I picked up my stack of flyers again and stopped counting who got the applause.

qa.q: What was Ines doing at the side table?
qa.a: Ines was writing letters to the council at a side table.

qa.q: Why did Paulo feel resentful of Rafael at first?
qa.a: Paulo felt small handing out flyers while the hall clapped for the loud speaker. Paulo noticed the quiet workers getting no applause.

qa.q: What changed Paulo's view of the work in the hall?
qa.a: Paulo saw Marta, Ines and Joaquim doing quiet jobs the meeting depended on, and heard Rafael name Marta's leaflets. Seeing varied contributions cooled the resentment.

qa.q: How might Marta have felt when Rafael thanked Marta's leaflets in front of everyone?
qa.a: Marta may have felt pleased and quietly proud that the unseen work was noticed. Shrugging and looking pleased suggests public thanks were unfamiliar.

grounding: Shows an observer seeing that a tenants' campaign needs speakers, printers, writers and funders, and how recognition eases resentment.

passage:
The community hall was warm on Sunday, and Mr. Kapoor gave the loudest speech about the school-crossing campaign. I’m Bhavna, and I watched from the third row. Leena, beside me, muttered, “We do the work, and they get the thanks.”
At the back Baljeet sat with a notebook, tallying donation slips and matching them to receipts. Sunita, at the side, was redrafting the petition for the city office.
I said quietly, “Without Baljeet’s accounts, no one would give a rupee. Without Sunita’s draft, the office wouldn’t read it.”
Leena looked around the hall. After the meeting she walked over and thanked Baljeet for the receipts. He looked surprised.

qa.q: What was Baljeet doing at the back of the hall?
qa.a: Baljeet was tallying donation slips and matching them to receipts.

qa.q: Why did Leena mutter that they do the work and others get the thanks?
qa.a: Leena felt overlooked and resentful, since the loud speeches got the attention while the quiet work went unnoticed.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's remark change for Leena?
qa.a: Bhavna pointed out how Baljeet's accounts and Sunita's draft made the campaign possible. Leena then looked around the hall and thanked Baljeet.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when Leena thanked him?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and pleased, since he looked surprised. Nobody had thanked him for the receipts before.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing that a campaign needs speakers, accountants and writers alike, and that recognising each role reduces resentment.

passage:
Hi Abhinav,
I've been thinking about Sunday's meeting. You said the clean-river campaign only moves because of the rallies, and that the 'office people' don't count. I got angry and said nothing, so here goes.
I've watched this group for a year. Meher does the accounts every night so our donations stay clean. Sanjay drives the old van to every site. Pritam dadi has written seventy letters to the council by hand. Laila designs the posters you hold up. None of them ever speaks on the mic.
You're a great speaker. The rallies matter. But when you say only speeches count, the quiet ones feel invisible, and some have stopped coming.
Can we thank them properly at the next meeting? Together?
Amandeep

qa.q: How many letters has Pritam dadi written to the council?
qa.a: Seventy letters, by hand.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when Abhinav dismissed the 'office people'?
qa.a: Amandeep felt angry but stayed silent at the meeting, then felt the need to speak up in writing.

qa.q: What does Amandeep suggest, and why would it help?
qa.a: Thanking the quiet contributors together at the next meeting, so they feel valued and the group's resentment eases.

qa.q: How might Meher feel hearing that only speeches count?
qa.a: Invisible and unappreciated, despite doing the accounts every night.

grounding: An observer of a campaign sees that quiet organisers, drivers, letter-writers and designers matter as much as speakers.

passage: Yogesh, thanks for asking about the tenants' campaign. I'm Ritu, and for a long time I thought the only people who mattered were the ones on stage. Our leader, Salma-ji, gives speeches that make grown men cry. But after two years of watching, I saw how many others it takes. Bose uncle, who never speaks, knows every tenant's name and phones each one before every meeting. Neelu types up the documents at night after her shift. A retired teacher sends us a small donation every month and has never come to a single rally. When some volunteers complained that Salma-ji got all the credit, I stood up and listed the others by name. The room went quiet, then clapped. Nobody's too small in a movement.

qa.q: What does Bose uncle do before every meeting?
qa.a: Phones each tenant.

qa.q: What did Ritu come to feel about the quiet workers over two years?
qa.a: Ritu came to feel appreciation and respect for the quiet workers, after first thinking only the people on stage mattered.

qa.q: How did Ritu reduce resentment when volunteers complained?
qa.a: By standing up and naming the quieter contributors, so everyone's work was recognised.

qa.q: How might Neelu feel being named at the meeting?
qa.a: Seen and appreciated for typing documents at night after her shift, work that usually goes unnoticed.

grounding: An observer comes to see that a movement needs quiet organisers, typists and donors, and naming them eases resentment.

passage: I've volunteered with the river-bank clean-up group in Guwahati for three years, and I've watched Pranav and Bhupen closely. Pranav is the one on the news, leading chants, giving interviews in his bright orange cap. Bhupen is the one nobody photographs. He arrives at five to count the sacks, fixes the broken boat engine and keeps the volunteer list on his phone. Last month a few people muttered that Pranav 'takes all the glory'. Pranav overheard. At the next gathering, he handed Bhupen the megaphone and said, 'Without him, there are no sacks, no boat, no us.' Bhupen went red and said only, 'Thank you. Now, the sacks.' People laughed. I can't know what Bhupen feels inside. But he came earlier than ever the next week.

qa.q: What does Bhupen fix?
qa.a: The broken boat engine.

qa.q: What does the narrator seem to feel watching Pranav hand Bhupen the megaphone?
qa.a: The narrator seems moved and hopeful, noting that Bhupen came earlier than ever afterwards, while admitting they can't know Bhupen's inner feelings.

qa.q: What did Pranav do to reduce the resentment in the group?
qa.a: He publicly credited Bhupen, handing him the megaphone and saying the group couldn't work without him.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt being handed the megaphone?
qa.a: Embarrassed but valued, going red and then turning it into a joke about the sacks.

grounding: A volunteer's account of a group where the visible speaker publicly credits a quiet worker, easing resentment.

passage:
Week one. At the first meeting of the campaign to save the night bus, Amandeep noticed only Harpal, who spoke standing on a chair and got every cheer. Dilnaz sat in a corner, writing names in a notebook. Amandeep privately thought she wasn't doing much.
Week three. The petition had 2,000 signatures. Amandeep asked who had organised the door-to-door rounds. It was Dilnaz, with a spreadsheet of every lane and every volunteer's free hours. Old Mr Fernandes, who couldn't walk far, had paid for the printing. A college student, Moumita, had written the letter to the transport office.
Week five. At the hearing, Harpal spoke brilliantly. When the room clapped, he pulled Dilnaz up to stand beside him. Amandeep clapped hardest for her, and felt a little ashamed of week one.

qa.q: How many signatures did the petition have in week three?
qa.a: The petition had 2,000 signatures.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep feel a little ashamed in week five?
qa.a: Amandeep had privately dismissed Dilnaz in week one, and now saw how much her quiet organising had achieved.

qa.q: What could a campaign do to reduce resentment between members?
qa.a: Name and thank the quieter roles, like Dilnaz's spreadsheet, Mr Fernandes's printing and Moumita's letter, as Harpal did by pulling Dilnaz up.

qa.q: What might it feel like for Dilnaz when Harpal pulls her up to stand beside him?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and seen, after weeks of work that few people noticed.

grounding: Amandeep, watching over five weeks, sees that the campaign needs organisers, funders and writers, not only its loudest speaker.
